title: The 40-Feature Wonder

scenario.situation: The team has built a classification model on an 80-row biomarker dataset with 40 features. Training accuracy is 100% and the team is presenting it to leadership next week as a breakthrough.
scenario.stakeholderBelief: The lead researcher argues that the model's strong cross-validated AUC on the training folds confirms the biological signal is real and the model is ready for clinical piloting.
scenario.question: Is the model as powerful as the team believes, or is something else going on?

decisions.prompt: Leadership wants you to validate the model before the presentation. How do you frame your investigation?

options.label: Audit the ratio of parameters to observations
options.detail: Examine whether the dataset has enough rows to support 40 features — flag the structural conditions that would make memorization inevitable regardless of apparent performance.
options.consequence: You immediately see that 40 features on 80 rows gives a parameters-to-observations ratio near 1:2. Even a random noise dataset would produce near-perfect fits at this ratio. This structural diagnosis sets up the right metric question — not whether performance looks good, but whether the dataset size can support any model of this complexity.

options.label: Confirm the signal with feature importance
options.detail: Rank features by importance scores to identify which biomarkers the model is relying on.
options.consequence: Feature importances look plausible and some align with domain knowledge — but you've only confirmed what the model memorized, not whether it can generalize. The structural overfitting problem remains invisible.
options.divergenceCost: Validated the model's internal logic without diagnosing whether the dataset can support any model of this complexity.

options.label: Benchmark against a simpler baseline on training data
options.detail: Compare the 40-feature model's training accuracy to a logistic regression with 3 features.
options.consequence: The complex model wins on training accuracy by a wide margin — of course it does. Training comparisons tell you nothing about generalization; you've reinforced the illusion while appearing rigorous.
options.divergenceCost: Compared models on the metric that always rewards complexity, bypassing the real structural question.

options.label: Expand the feature set with interaction terms
options.detail: Add interaction terms and derived features to capture more biological complexity before evaluating.
options.consequence: Training accuracy stays at 100% — naturally, with even more parameters than rows. You've deepened the overfitting hole while appearing to be thorough.
options.divergenceCost: Added complexity to an already over-parameterized model, making the core structural problem worse.

decisions.prompt: The structural audit raises a red flag. Now you need to choose a metric to surface whether the model is memorizing or learning. Which do you use?

artifact.title: Training accuracy by model complexity
artifact.caption: Training accuracy climbs steadily with complexity and hits 100% at 40 features. Is this the right lens?

options.label: Training accuracy across complexity levels
options.detail: Plot training accuracy as features are added to the model.
options.consequence: Training accuracy rises monotonically to 100% — exactly what you'd expect whether the model is learning or memorizing. This metric is structurally blind to overfitting and cannot distinguish the two cases.
options.divergenceCost: Chose a metric that always rewards adding features, making the diagnosis impossible from the start.

options.label: Held-out test accuracy across complexity levels
options.detail: Reserve 20% of the data before any modeling; plot test-set accuracy at each complexity level.
options.consequence: The held-out curve peaks early — around 5 features — and then collapses to near 50% at 40 features. The gap between training and test accuracy is the unmistakable fingerprint of memorization, not learning, and it cannot be argued away.

artifact.title: Test accuracy by model complexity (held-out set)
artifact.caption: Generalization peaks at 5 features and degrades to near-random at full complexity — confirming memorization, not biological signal.

decisions.prompt: Held-out accuracy collapses at high complexity. What do you tell the lead researcher before the presentation?

options.label: "The model is overfit and the biological signal doesn't exist — this dataset can't support any meaningful model."
options.detail: Declare the underlying signal invalid and advise cancelling the research line.
options.consequence: The overfitting diagnosis is correct, but you've conflated 'this model failed' with 'no signal exists.' The 5-feature model showed a genuine, if modest, test accuracy lift. Writing off the research direction goes beyond what the evidence supports and may shut down a tractable path.
options.divergenceCost: Treated a modeling failure as evidence that the underlying biology is uninformative — a logical leap the data doesn't support.

options.label: "The 100% training accuracy is a memorization artifact — but the 5-feature model shows a real, modest test-set lift. Let's present that as a promising early signal and recommend a targeted data-collection plan before any clinical use."
options.detail: Report the finding, name the structural mechanism, and propose a confirmatory path.
options.consequence: You've separated the modeling failure from the question of whether a biological signal exists, given leadership an honest interim finding, and charted a concrete next step. The presentation becomes a credible candidate hypothesis rather than either a premature breakthrough or a dead end.

insight: The 100% training accuracy was a structural inevitability, not a discovery: with 40 features and only 80 rows, the model had nearly one parameter per observation and could memorize any label assignment. The lead researcher's cross-validated AUC was a credible-sounding red herring — internal validation on the same toxic ratio still disguises memorization. The held-out test curve exposed the real picture: generalization peaked at 5 features and fell to near-random at full complexity. The lesson is that model validity must be diagnosed from data geometry first, and that even rigorous-sounding validation metrics can fail when the parameters-to-observations ratio is structurally broken.
